title: A weekly circle
tomorrow: what do you even say when you visit someone who's sick?

cards: A group chat goes silent for weeks, then lights up the second someone types: same time next week? Some things only happen when people keep showing up. Amira quit her Wednesday study circle in the fall.
Too busy, she said, and she can read on her own. So does a circle really matter, or is studying alone just as good?

teach.b: The tradition answers in a report in Sahih Muslim.

No group gathers in one of the houses of God, reciting the Book and studying it together, but four things happen: tranquility, sakina, comes down on them; mercy covers them; angels surround them; and God mentions them among those with Him.
Notice it isn't only about learning. It's about what settles on the room. And why weekly?
In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Mas'ud gave his reminders every Thursday. People asked him to make it every day. He said no: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ spaced out his teaching so they wouldn't grow bored.
A circle that meets once a week, on purpose, so people keep coming back. Now a neighbor.

Jordan's grandmother goes to a Wednesday night Bible study, and there's a line Christians quote for exactly this, from Matthew's Gospel, in the King James words: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them."
What's shared: the sense that something is present when people gather that isn't there when you sit alone.

What's honestly different: in Matthew, Jesus speaks of himself in their midst, and Christians hear Christ present; in the hadith, it's tranquility, mercy, angels and God's remembrance, and Muslims don't speak of the Prophet being there.
Two traditions, each in its own words, both pulling up a chair.

how: Muslims gather in weekly study circles (halaqas) at mosques, campuses and homes, reading a passage of the Qur'an or hadith together and talking it through, often with a teacher.

o: a group that meets on a set day to study together
a prayer said walking in a ring around the Ka'ba
a yearly retreat for memorizing the Qur'an

games.q: the circle, two ways — tap the pairs.

s: a report says studying together brings tranquility, mercy and angels
Sahih Muslim: and God mentions them among those with Him.
Ibn Mas'ud taught every day, because more is always better
he taught on Thursdays and refused to go daily, so people wouldn't tire.
Matthew 18:20 and the hadith say exactly the same thing
both say something is present when people gather; Matthew names Jesus in their midst, the hadith names tranquility, mercy and angels.

games.q: you run a study group, and two members want to meet every night instead of weekly. what would Ibn Mas'ud say?
o: keep it weekly, so people don't tire and keep coming.
every night. more study is more reward, no limit.
cancel it. studying alone covers the same ground.
games.why: Ibn Mas'ud turned down daily reminders, following the Prophet, who spaced out his teaching so people wouldn't grow bored.

practice: Bring to mind one person you'd study with, or one circle you've drifted from. Send them a short message now: a question about something you read, or simply, same time next week?
If there's no one yet, write down one place a circle might be waiting: a mosque, a library, a friend's kitchen table.

wordCard.voice: A weekly circle, a halaqa: people who meet on a set day to read and study together, and on whom, the report says, tranquility comes down.

orig.note: Arabic: halaqa, a ring or circle; the word for a study circle.

carryVoice: Keep it near: every week, the circle is where the settling happens. One day left in the week's turn.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2699 (no people gather in a house of God reciting and studying the Book but tranquility descends, mercy covers them, angels surround them, and God mentions them among those with Him)
Sahih al-Bukhari 70 (Ibn Mas'ud's talks every Thursday; he declined to make them daily, as the Prophet spaced out teaching lest they grow bored); see also 68

sources.q: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
